cards.title: Model checking Markov chains with continuous observations
cards.formal: Can finite-state, discrete-time hidden Markov models with continuously distributed observations be model-checked efficiently? The source asks for verification of specifications about such probabilistic models after establishing a polynomial-time equivalence test. It does not identify a specification language, its observation predicates, a qualitative versus quantitative probability question, or the intended complexity bound. Consequently this record defines the stochastic model and known equivalence result, but does not substitute a chosen temporal logic or threshold problem for the source’s unresolved request.
cards.why: Would clarify which verification guarantees remain computationally accessible when a finite probabilistic system emits real measurements rather than letters from a finite alphabet.
cards.status_note: Read the conference model, profile encodings, Theorem 12 and conclusion, and checked the full version. Exact-title and continuous-observation model-checking searches through 12 September 2026 found no later result that supplies and settles a unique interpretation of this broad question.

sentences: A finite hidden Markov model can emit real observations at discrete transitions.
The source represents their densities by finite symbolic profiles and proves a polynomial-time equivalence test.
It then asks whether specifications of these models can also be checked efficiently.
The specification language, observation predicates, probability semantics and requested complexity remain unspecified.
The revised card separates those missing choices from the established equivalence result and defines the probabilistic model without prescribing an algorithm.

cards.definitions: A hidden Markov model has a finite state set Q and an observation space Σ equipped with a σ-algebra of measurable sets and a reference measure λ. A nonnegative observation-density matrix Ψ assigns a |Q|×|Q| matrix to each observation x. The matrix P with P_ij=∫_Σ Ψ_ij(x)dλ(x) is stochastic: every row sums to one. Conditional on state i, the probability of moving to j while emitting an observation in a measurable set A is ∫_A Ψ_ij(x)dλ(x). Time advances by one discrete step at each transition; a real observation is not automatically a holding time. With an initial row probability vector π, the probability of an observation cylinder A₁×⋯×A_t is π(∫_{A₁}Ψdλ)⋯(∫_{A_t}Ψdλ)1, where 1 is the all-ones column vector. These cylinders determine the trace distribution on infinite observation sequences. The source assumes a topological observation space whose nonempty open sets are measurable with positive measure, and piecewise-continuous density functions. Its concrete example uses Σ=R and Lebesgue measure. The finite input represents densities by profiles: strings giving a function type and rational parameters, with rational linear combinations. The example profile language Γ_GEM includes Gaussian densities, exponential densities and interval-supported monomials x^k 1_[a,b)(x), with rational endpoints and nonnegative integer k. Valid HMM inputs promise nonnegative densities and stochastic normalization, even when profile expressions use signed coefficients. A profile language is linearly decomposable when, from any finite collection of profiles, an algorithm can compute a basis chosen from that collection and rational coefficients expressing the others, in polynomial time in their encoded lengths; functions equal almost everywhere are identified. Two initial distributions are equivalent when they induce equal probabilities for every measurable set of infinite observation traces. This is the proved comparison task. Model checking would instead receive a specification and test its satisfaction under a stated probabilistic semantics; those semantics and the specification encoding are absent from the question.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete acceptance condition first needs an exact specification language, observation-predicate representation, probability semantics and output requirement, and a running-time bound in the encoded model, specification and any accuracy parameters. A solution must then prove the bound for all promised inputs or establish a matching impossibility under explicitly stated assumptions. This record does not yet define that proposition. Deciding equality of two whole trace distributions, handling one chosen logic, or numerically evaluating a particular observed sequence does not by itself resolve the unspecified source question.

context_blocks.title: Continuous observations with finite hidden state
context_blocks.text: The state transition mechanism is finite, but each transition can emit a real measurement from a distribution depending on the hidden transition. This captures observations such as elapsed time or resource use without replacing the system by an arbitrary continuous-state process.

context_blocks.title: The established theorem is equivalence
context_blocks.text: Theorem 12 decides equality of the induced observation laws in polynomial time for rational initial distributions and a linearly decomposable profile language. The paper establishes that its Gaussian, exponential and piecewise-polynomial language has the required property.

context_blocks.title: Why equivalence does not specify verification
context_blocks.text: Equality of two probability measures and evaluation of a specification are different tasks. The theorem does not provide a language for describing events or a numerical representation for the probability of a specified event.

context_blocks.title: What is still missing from the extracted question
context_blocks.text: The conclusion asks about efficient model checking without fixing a logic or probability query. The full version retains this broad question. Choosing, for example, observation thresholds, time bounds or a temporal logic would produce additional mathematical choices not settled by that passage.

cards.context:
The state transition mechanism is finite, but each transition can emit a real measurement from a distribution depending on the hidden transition. This captures observations such as elapsed time or resource use without replacing the system by an arbitrary continuous-state process.

Theorem 12 decides equality of the induced observation laws in polynomial time for rational initial distributions and a linearly decomposable profile language. The paper establishes that its Gaussian, exponential and piecewise-polynomial language has the required property.

Equality of two probability measures and evaluation of a specification are different tasks. The theorem does not provide a language for describing events or a numerical representation for the probability of a specified event.

The conclusion asks about efficient model checking without fixing a logic or probability query. The full version retains this broad question. Choosing, for example, observation thresholds, time bounds or a temporal logic would produce additional mathematical choices not settled by that passage.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
